## 🌟 Summary
**v8.4.165 improves package compatibility, export and inference reliability, and dataset handling, with several targeted fixes for model outputs and vision workflows.**

## 📊 Key Changes
- 📦 **Cleaner Python wheel installation (current PR #26408):** Test files are no longer installed as a top-level `tests` package, avoiding conflicts with other projects. Tests remain in the source distribution so Conda builds can still run them.
- 🚀 **More reliable exports and inference:** ONNX export now checks that the requested opset is high enough for the model and reports a clear error if it is not. Windows OpenVINO inference also avoids a CPU instruction path that could crash on some machines.
- 📐 **Improved depth and semantic outputs:** Depth resizing now follows the same alignment convention used during training and validation. Saved semantic prediction masks are restored to the original image size without letterbox padding, and invalid semantic class IDs are flagged during dataset scanning.
- 🧹 **Safer, more consistent dataset processing:** Fixes cover whitespace-only labels, distinct segmentation polygons that share a bounding box, repeatable classification dataset splits, older Albumentations versions, and nested paths in COCO/LVIS conversion. Multispectral conversion now keeps source images if outputs collide or fail to write.
- 🎯 **More accurate vision utilities:** Corrected flips for left-top-width-height boxes, kept tracked pose keypoints colored by track ID, improved distance-calculation selection, and fixed class histories in analytics charts.
- 🛠️ **Documentation and CI updates:** Clarified Platform annotation and image-search guidance, corrected Ascend device mappings, and updated runner versions and test behavior.

## 🎯 Purpose & Impact
- ✅ **Fewer installation surprises:** The wheel no longer shadows other packages’ `tests` imports, while source-based Conda builds retain the tests they need.
- 🧪 **Clearer failure feedback and more dependable deployment:** Unsupported ONNX opsets fail early with an actionable message, and Windows OpenVINO is less prone to native crashes.
- 📊 **More trustworthy training and evaluation:** Dataset issues are caught earlier, repeated classification splits stay consistent, and saved semantic masks and depth outputs better match their intended image geometry.
- 🛡️ **Reduced risk of losing data:** Failed or colliding multispectral conversions no longer silently delete original images.

summary: On July 24, 2025, Microsoft Research Asia – Singapore (MSRA – Singapore) opened its doors as Microsoft’s first research lab in Southeast Asia. The launch built on more than two decades of collaboration between Microsoft Research Asia and Singapore’s universities, research institutes, and government agencies. It marked a shift to a closer, more integrated relationship aimed at supporting Singapore’s innovation ecosystem and advancing the development and beneficial use of AI. “When we established Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore one year ago, our vision was not simply to open another research lab. It was to build a bridge connecting Microsoft’s frontier AI research with Singapore’s world-class universities, forward-thinking government agencies, and dynamic industry ecosystem. One year in, what gives me the greatest confidence is not just the research we have produced, but the depth of partnership we have built. That is the foundation on which lasting impact is built.”— Dr. Lidong Zhou, corporate vice president at Microsoft and managing director of Microsoft Research Asia Established in 1998, MSRA has a presence in Beijing, Shanghai, Vancouver, and Tokyo, along with Singapore. The Singapore lab strengthens the collaboration with local partners and extends the scientific and societal impact of Microsoft’s global research community. Over the past year, the Singapore lab has grown its team, deepened partnerships, and explored how frontier AI research can create real-world value. Guided by its mission to advance frontier AI for humanity, its work spans four pillars: next-generation AI models and agentic systems, domain-specific AI for real-world impact, AI-native research practices, and ecosystem and talent development. From frontier research to real-world impact – and back Research has its greatest impact when it moves beyond the laboratory into practice: in health and medicine, enterprises, and the daily operations of organizations solving real problems. MSRA – Singapore aims to do just that through a two-way exchange: partners bring domain expertise, real-world data, and operational challenges, while the lab contributes frontier research and engineering capabilities. Together, they translate fundamental advances into practical solutions, while surfacing new questions that feed back into research in a kind of research-to-impact flywheel. Advances in AI foundations enable more capable models and agentic systems that can reason, plan, use tools, and collaborate with people. These capabilities create new opportunities for AI-native innovation. In turn, real-world applications reveal limitations and generate new questions, feeding insights back into foundational research and sustaining a continuous cycle of discovery, application, and learning. Healthcare offers an early example of the lab’s research-to-impact model. Research on multimodal healthcare AI and self-evolving diagnostic agents is deployed and extended through partnerships across Singapore’s healthcare ecosystem. The lab is collaborating on multimodal and agentic AI approaches to support clinical decision-making, unlock insights from complex medical data, and advance research in disease diagnosis, risk assessment, and personalized care, with the longer-term goal of enabling meaningful real-world use. Beyond healthcare, the lab is working with organizations across financial services, education, and technology to explore how frontier AI can address sector-specific needs and operational challenges. “Over the past year, the lab has become an integral part of both Microsoft’s local ecosystem and Singapore’s broader innovation community. Its progress demonstrates the value of establishing a sustained research presence in Singapore.”— Wee Luen Chia, managing director, Microsoft Singapore Singapore has made AI a national priority through its National AI Strategy 2.0 (opens in new tab), which focuses on deploying industry-transforming AI, advancing frontier research in AI foundations, and developing responsible, socially beneficial applications. These priorities span areas including healthcare, education, finance, and Smart Nation (opens in new tab) services. MSRA – Singapore’s research portfolio aligns with these priorities, with a particular focus on building AI systems that are reliable and trustworthy across Southeast Asian contexts. The Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) has been a foundational partner. It supported the lab’s establishment and continues to support joint PhD training through the Industrial Postgraduate Programme (IPP). The relationship has since grown into strategic collaboration. In February 2026, EDB co-hosted an Executive Roundtable on AI in Logistics and Transportation, bringing together more than ten regional industry leaders to explore sectoral challenges. “Singapore is building deep research capabilities to push the boundaries of AI and other frontier technologies. Microsoft Research Asia – Singapore is an important partner in this effort. Since its launch in 2025, the lab has brought Microsoft’s global research expertise closer to our ecosystem, partnering academia, industry, and government to advance frontier AI research and translate it into real-world applications in areas such as healthcare. MSRA is also developing the next generation of AI research talent who can create meaningful impact for our economy and society.”— Low Jin Yong, senior vice president and co-head, Digital Industry Singapore Government engagement extends beyond EDB. In July 2025, IMDA (opens in new tab) co-hosted Microsoft Research Asia Singapore Day (opens in new tab)— Advancing Industrial AI, a full-day event spanning healthcare AI, interactive world simulators, AI agents, and societal AI. MSRA – Singapore has also engaged with the Ministry of Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Health. From enduring partnerships to shared discovery In addition to its deep ties with government agencies, MSRA has built strong connections with Singapore’s academic community, supporting more than 75 research projects with Singapore institutions since 2004. The opening of the Singapore lab has brought new engagements, with nine new projects in its first year with National University of Singapore (NUS) and Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU) across healthcare AI, robotics, AI systems, and multi-agent systems. A landmark example is the five-year Framework Research Agreement (opens in new tab) with NUS, announced in 2025, which provides a platform for joint AI research, talent development, and academic exchange. It defines shared research priorities in healthcare, societal AI, spatial intelligence, and data-intensive computing alongside an annual NUS–MSRA Academic Symposium that brings researchers from both organizations together to shape the collaboration agenda. “This partnership creates new opportunities for frontier research, talent development, and knowledge exchange, strengthening connections across academia, industry, and the broader innovation ecosystem.”— Professor Liu Bin, deputy president (Research and Technology), National University of Singapore The collaboration is already producing concrete research across several frontier areas. NUS Assistant Professor Mike Shou and MSRA’s Xinxing Xu are developing unified multimodal AI for healthcare. NUS assistant professor Yang You and MSRA distinguished scientist Furu Wei are studying systems foundations for diffusion-based language models. NUS assistant professor Jialin Li is working with MSRA on rigorous distributed agreement in multi-agent systems and verifiable machine learning systems. “Whether during my visit to the Systems Research Group in Beijing or through our ongoing collaborations, I have been impressed by how deeply MSRA researchers engage with difficult problems and how openly they exchange ideas. For young faculty and students, it is a rare environment to explore ambitious ideas. “— Jialin Li, Sung Kah Kay Assistant Professor, School of Computing, National University of Singapore, MSRA StarTrack Scholar The NUS–Microsoft Research Asia AI Summer School has reached more than 300 students since its launch in 2025, attracting participants from Singapore, Southeast Asia, and beyond. Through three days of lectures, hands-on workshops, and small-group discussions, the program creates a forum for researchers and students to engage with emerging AI questions and scholars shaping the field. The 2025 program featured a keynote by Doug Burger, technical fellow and corporate vice president of Microsoft, on the AI revolution. Ahead of the 2026 Summer School, Lidong Zhou delivered a lecture on system intelligence, helping frame the conversations that followed. “I have seen the NUS–MSRA partnership grow through sustained collaboration in AI research and talent development. What makes this partnership especially meaningful is the opportunity to bring together researchers and students from both communities to learn from one another, pursue new ideas, and create lasting impact together.”— Tulika Mitra, dean, NUS School of Computing Beyond NUS, Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore has built connections across Singapore’s research community, including with NTU, Singapore Management University (SMU) (opens in new tab), Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), and other institutions. Research arising from these partnerships has already been published at leading venues, including the International Conference on Learning Representations (opens in new tab) (ICLR) and the Conference on Language Modeling (opens in new tab) (COLM). From early exposure to research leadership: Cultivating Singapore’s next generation of AI talent For Microsoft Research Asia, talent development is not a standalone program but a long-term investment in Singapore’s research and innovation capacity, supporting a comprehensive talent pipeline spanning internships, joint PhD supervision, visiting scholar programs, and fellowship initiatives. Through these opportunities, students and early-career researchers gain access to world-class mentorship, a curiosity-driven culture, frontier research challenges, and a global network connecting academia, industry, and real-world applications. What makes this model distinctive is its continuity. Students may engage with Microsoft Research Asia through workshops or summer schools, gain hands-on experience through its flagship research initiative, Microsoft Research Asia Stars of Tomorrow Internship Program, or pursue doctoral research through joint PhD programs. Some participants later return as faculty collaborators, mentors, or research leaders. Together, these programs form a connected pathway that supports researchers at successive stages of development. The IPP represents a sustained form of collaboration, enabling PhD students to conduct long-term research under joint mentorship from academia and industry. Qiming Huang, the first IPP student at MSRA — Singapore, is co-supervised by NUS professor Mike Shou and MSRA researcher Xinxing Xu. Through the program, Huang worked closely with researchers from both institutions, gaining exposure to academic rigor and industry-driven research. At CVPR 2026 (opens in new tab), one of the world’s leading conferences in AI and computer vision, Qiming Huang’s paper on RobotSeg – a foundation model for robot segmentation in image and video – was selected for an oral presentation. “Working alongside researchers from both Microsoft Research Asia and NUS changed how I approach AI research. Beyond technical guidance, I learned to frame ambitious questions, collaborate across disciplines, and think about the real-world impact of research— Qiming Huang, IPP student from National University of Singapore NTU assistant professor Jianfei Yang, embodies the continuous collaborative opportunities enabled by Microsoft Research Asia. As a student, Yang’s team won the Beauty of Programming competition, an experience that inspired him to pursue a PhD and begin an academic career. Over the years, he watched many of his classmates and close friends grow into outstanding researchers through MSRA programs. Today, he collaborates with MSRA researchers in robotics and jointly supervises students through the IPP, creating for the next generation the same opportunities that inspired his own journey. “Although I never interned at Microsoft Research Asia myself, it always felt close. Having the opportunity to work alongside a research lab that inspired so many researchers of my generation, and now to co-mentor students together, is both meaningful and rewarding.”— Jianfei Yang, assistant professor, director of Multimodal embodied AI and Robotic Systems (MARS) Lab, Nanyang Technological University NTU associate professor Ziwei Liu, himself a former MSRA intern, recently saw one of his students become the only Asia-based recipient of the Microsoft Research global Fellowship award for 2025–2026. “As a former intern, I have seen how an environment that brings together world-class researchers, open scientific exchange, and ambitious young talent can shape the next generation of researchers. It is especially meaningful to see my own students now benefit from these opportunities.”— Ziwei Liu, associate professor, College of Computing and Data Science, Nanyang Technological University The Stars of Tomorrow Internship Program has engaged more than 90 students from Singapore-based institutions over the years. For many students, these internships serve as a gateway to frontier research and help bridge the gap between academic study and real-world innovation. For exceptional doctoral students, the Microsoft Research Asia Fellowship provides another pathway for growth, recognition, mentorship, and access to Microsoft’s global research community. Since the program began, 13 students from Singapore-based universities have received the fellowship, many of whom have gone on to become professors, industry research leaders, and technology entrepreneurs around the world. The next phase: Scaling what works As Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore enters its second year, the focus is shifting from building foundations to scaling the strongest models of collaboration and demonstrating their impact more broadly. One year ago, the lab opened with a mission to advance frontier AI in close partnership with the ecosystem around it. That mission is already taking shape through joint research, talent development, and the first partnerships connecting lab work to real-world challenges. The year ahead is about scaling what works. By deepening these connections, Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore can bring more frontier research into practice and create meaningful value for Singapore, the wider region, industry, and society.
